faq: What does this tool calculate?
Coordinates of points at even bearing intervals on a circle of chosen radius around a centre, each projected on the sphere by the destination formula.
Do I need an account?
No — centre, radius and count in; ring out.
Can I use the result for professional work?
For sampling designs, coverage checks and geofence drafts, yes — the geometry is the sphere's own. Legal boundaries remain surveyed instruments' work.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
Ring points inherit the centre's accuracy. Their relative geometry is exact regardless — a perfect circle around an approximate centre.
Can I choose the starting bearing?
The ring's rotation is yours to set where the tool exposes it — align point one to the feature that matters.
Miles or kilometres?
Both, per site convention.
Huge radii?
The sphere handles them — a 5,000 km 'ring' is a small circle around the antipode's neighbourhood, geometrically sound and practically a thought experiment.
Points inside the circle too?
Concentric rings: generate at fractions of the radius and merge — the sampling-grid pattern built from circles.
Polygon export?
The points list in order is the polygon — copy it into your GIS or GeoJSON by hand for small counts.
Spacing between neighbours?
Chord distance follows from the radius and count (2R sin(π/count)) — the coverage question's real number, computable from the same inputs.
